content: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a premalignant lesion that is classified histologically into three grades: CIN 1, CIN 2, and CIN 3. If left untreated, CIN 2 and CIN 3 (collectively referred to as CIN 2+) have the potential to progress to invasive cervical cancer. The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified three primary treatment modalities for CIN, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. These include cryotherapy, large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ, also known as loop electrosurgical excision procedure or LEEP), and cold knife conization (CKC). This guideline builds upon the 2011 WHO recommendations on the use of cryotherapy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. It provides updated recommendations for the use of cryotherapy, LEEP, and CKC in the treatment of histologically confirmed CIN 2+ lesions. Additionally, it includes specific recommendations for the management of histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). In 2009, the WHO committed to revising the 2006 edition of the Comprehensive Cervical Cancer Control: A Guide to Essential Practice (C4-GEP). One of the key updates identified was the need to revise the chapter on screening and treatment of precancerous cervical lesions to reflect the latest evidence and practices. The guideline development process involved multiple expert groups, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the Methods Group (MG), and the External Review Group (ERG). These groups collaborated extensively between 2010 and 2013 to develop and refine the recommendations. This process included systematic reviews of the literature, evidence grading using the GRADE methodology, and iterative discussions to finalize the recommendations. To ensure transparency and manage conflicts of interest, all participating experts were required to complete WHO Declaration of Interest (DOI) forms. These declarations were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat and the Office of the Legal Counsel. Relevant conflicts of interest were disclosed in the guideline, and all experts were permitted to participate in the process. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of the GDG, MG, and ERG, as well as the support of external organizations such as the Flanders International Cooperation Agency (FICA), the Institut National du Cancer (INCa) in France, and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (GAVI), which provided funding for the development of this document. This guideline aims to provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of precancerous cervical lesions and adenocarcinoma in situ, with a focus on improving outcomes in resource-limited settings.
